source.title: How Courts and Justice Work
source.attribution: A Reborn guide drawing on the United Nations, the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, the US Courts, the UK Judiciary and the National Registry of Exonerations.
source.notes: Written by Reborn; no text copied. References: United Nations, What is the Rule of Law, https://www.un.org/ruleoflaw/what-is-the-rule-of-law/; UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, https://www.ohchr.org/en/instruments-mechanisms/instruments/international-covenant-civil-and-political-rights; United States Courts, Criminal Cases, https://www.uscourts.gov/about-federal-courts/types-cases/criminal-cases; Courts and Tribunals Judiciary, About the judiciary, https://www.judiciary.uk/about-the-judiciary/; National Registry of Exonerations, https://www.law.umich.edu/special/exoneration/; Criminal Cases Review Commission, https://ccrc.gov.uk/

cards.title: Courts turn disputes and accusations into fair, reasoned decisions
cards.body:
When someone is accused of a crime, or two people cannot settle a dispute, societies need a fair way to decide what happened and what should follow. That is the job of courts and the wider justice system.

This guide explains the big ideas: the rule of law, what happens at arrest, the presumption of innocence and the burden of proof. It covers the difference between criminal and civil cases, the roles of judges, juries and lawyers, and how evidence and witnesses are handled. Then it looks at sentencing, appeals, wrongful convictions and how systems differ around the world.

One important note: rules differ a lot by country, and even within countries. This guide is general education, not legal advice. If you face a legal problem, speak to a qualified lawyer.
cards.apply_it: Think of one court case you have seen in the news. As you read, notice which ideas from this guide it involved.

quiz.question: What is this guide intended to give you?
options: General education about how justice systems work
Legal advice for your own case
A list of every country's laws
Instructions for representing yourself in court
quiz.explanation: The guide explains general ideas only. Rules vary by country, and anyone with a real legal issue should see a qualified lawyer.

cards.title: Justice systems differ by country, but many share common roots
cards.body:
There is no single worldwide justice system. Each country, and sometimes each state or region, has its own laws, courts and procedures.

Many systems fall into two broad families. Common law systems, found in England, the United States, India, Australia and other places influenced by English law, rely heavily on past court decisions called precedents, alongside laws passed by parliaments.

Civil law systems, found in much of Europe, Latin America and parts of Asia and Africa, rely mainly on detailed written codes. Judges apply the code to each case.

Other systems draw on religious law, customary law or a mix of traditions. Many countries combine elements of several. That is why examples in this guide are only examples. Local rules always come first.
cards.apply_it: Find out which legal family your country mainly belongs to: common law, civil law or a mix.

quiz.question: What do common law systems rely on heavily?
options: Past court decisions called precedents, alongside laws
quiz.explanation: Common law systems give great weight to precedents, which are earlier decisions by courts on similar issues.

cards.title: The rule of law means everyone, including the powerful, must follow the law
cards.body:
The rule of law is the idea that a country is governed by clear, public laws that apply to everyone equally, rather than by the wishes of whoever holds power.

The United Nations describes it as a principle where all people, institutions and the state itself are accountable to laws that are publicly made, equally enforced and independently judged, and that are consistent with human rights.

In practice, this means a president, a police officer and an ordinary citizen should all face the same rules. Laws should be known in advance, so people can follow them. And disputes should be decided by independent courts, not by force.

No country lives up to this perfectly. But it is the yardstick used to judge whether a justice system is fair.
cards.apply_it: Think of a news story where a powerful person faced the courts. Did the rule of law seem to work?

quiz.question: What does the rule of law mean?
options: Rulers can make up rules as they go
Everyone, including the state, is accountable to public, fairly applied laws
Only judges must follow the law
quiz.explanation: The rule of law means clear, public laws that apply equally to everyone, judged by independent courts.

cards.title: Independent judges protect people from misuse of power
cards.body:
Most democracies split power into three branches. The legislature, like a parliament, makes laws. The executive, like a government, runs the country and enforces laws. The judiciary, the courts, interprets laws and settles disputes.

This separation of powers means no single group holds all the power. Courts can check whether the government itself is acting lawfully.

For this to work, judges must be independent. They should not be punished or rewarded for their decisions, should be protected from political pressure and should decide cases only on the law and the evidence.

Countries protect independence in different ways, such as secure jobs until retirement age, fixed salaries and independent appointment bodies. When governments pressure or replace judges for political reasons, it is a warning sign for the rule of law.
cards.apply_it: Look up how judges are appointed in your country.

quiz.question: Why is judicial independence important?
options: So judges can do whatever they like
So judges decide cases on law and evidence, free from political pressure
So courts can make new taxes
quiz.explanation: Independent judges can rule fairly, even against the government, because they are protected from pressure.

cards.title: Laws come from constitutions, parliaments and court decisions
cards.body:
Where do laws actually come from? Usually from a few places.

Many countries have a constitution, a top-level set of rules about how the state works and what rights people have. Other laws must fit within it. Some constitutions are written in one document, while the UK's is spread across many laws and traditions.

Parliaments or legislatures pass laws called statutes or acts. These cover crimes, taxes, contracts and much more.

In common law countries, judges' decisions also create law through precedent. When a higher court decides a question, lower courts usually follow it.

International treaties, such as human rights agreements, can also shape national law, depending on how each country brings them in.
cards.apply_it: Find out whether your country has a written constitution, and what one right it guarantees.

quiz.question: What is a statute?
options: A law passed by a parliament or legislature
quiz.explanation: Statutes, also called acts, are laws passed by a legislature such as a parliament or congress.

cards.title: Police usually need a good reason to arrest someone
cards.body:
An arrest is when police take someone into custody because they suspect the person has committed a crime. In most democracies, police cannot arrest people at random.

The exact test differs by country. In England and Wales, police generally need reasonable grounds to suspect an offence and to believe an arrest is necessary. In the United States, police generally need probable cause. Other countries use different standards.

Police may also stop and question people, or search them, under specific rules. These powers have limits, and how they are used is often debated, especially when some groups are stopped far more than others.

Being arrested does not mean someone is guilty. It is the start of an investigation. Many people who are arrested are never charged.
cards.apply_it: Look up what standard police in your country must meet before making an arrest.

quiz.question: What does being arrested mean?
options: Police suspect the person and have taken them into custody
The person has been proven guilty
The person must go to prison
quiz.explanation: An arrest is based on suspicion and starts an investigation. It is not a finding of guilt.

cards.title: People who are arrested usually have key rights, but they vary
cards.body:
International human rights law, including the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, sets out basic protections for anyone who is detained. Many countries build on these.

Common rights include being told why you are being arrested, being able to speak to a lawyer, not being held for long without being charged or brought before a judge, and being treated humanely. Many systems also protect a right not to incriminate yourself.

The details differ a lot. In the US, the Miranda warning tells people they have a right to remain silent. In England and Wales, the police caution warns that staying silent about something you later rely on in court may harm your defence.

If you are ever arrested, asking for a lawyer is usually a sensible first step.
cards.apply_it: Find out what the police warning or caution says in your country.

quiz.question: Which is a common right for someone who has been arrested?
options: To be told why they are arrested and to speak to a lawyer
To see the police officer's diary
quiz.explanation: Most systems give arrested people the right to know why they are held and to get legal advice, though details vary.

cards.title: If police stop you, staying calm and polite protects you
cards.body:
Being stopped by police can be stressful, whether you have done anything wrong or not. Some general tips apply in many places, but laws differ, so check what applies where you live.

Stay calm and keep your hands visible. Arguing or running can make things more dangerous and may be a crime in itself.

You can usually ask, politely, whether you are free to go, and why you have been stopped. In many places you can ask for an officer's name or number.

In many countries you have the right not to answer questions about a crime without a lawyer. But in some places you must give your name or show ID in certain situations.

If you believe police treated you unfairly, you can usually complain later through an official body.
cards.apply_it: Look up what your local rules say about showing ID to police.

quiz.question: What is a sensible thing to do if police stop you?
options: Stay calm, keep hands visible and politely ask if you are free to go
Refuse to say anything ever, even your name, everywhere
quiz.explanation: Calm, polite behaviour keeps everyone safer. Any complaint can be made later through official channels.

cards.title: After arrest, police must charge, release or bring a suspect before a court
cards.body:
Police cannot usually hold someone forever. Most countries set time limits on detention without charge or without seeing a judge. In England and Wales, the usual limit is 24 hours, which can be extended in some cases. Other countries have different limits, and terrorism cases often have special rules.

During this time, police may interview the suspect, gather evidence and talk to witnesses. Then a decision is made.

The suspect may be released with no further action, released while the investigation continues, given a warning or caution, or formally charged with a crime. A charge means the case is going to court.

In many countries, the decision to charge serious crimes is made or checked by prosecutors, not just police.
cards.apply_it: Think about why time limits on police detention might matter for protecting innocent people.

quiz.question: What does it mean when someone is charged?
options: They are formally accused and the case is going to court
They are free with no further action
quiz.explanation: A charge is a formal accusation that sends the case to court. It is still not a finding of guilt.

cards.title: Everyone is presumed innocent until proven guilty
cards.body:
The presumption of innocence is one of the most important principles in criminal justice. It is in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and in the laws of most countries.

It means a person accused of a crime is treated as innocent unless and until the prosecution proves their guilt in a fair trial. The accused does not have to prove they are innocent.

This protects people from being punished just because they were accused, or because they look suspicious, or because the public is angry.

It is also why news reports use words like alleged and accused. Calling someone guilty before a verdict can unfairly affect a trial, and in some countries it can even be contempt of court.
cards.apply_it: Next time you read about an arrest, notice whether the report uses words like alleged and accused.

quiz.question: What does the presumption of innocence mean?
options: The accused must prove they are innocent
The accused is treated as innocent until guilt is proven in a fair trial
quiz.explanation: The prosecution must prove guilt. Until then, the accused is treated as innocent.

cards.title: In criminal cases, guilt must be proven beyond reasonable doubt
cards.body:
The burden of proof is about who has to prove something, and how strongly. In criminal cases, the burden is on the prosecution, which acts for the state.

In many common law countries, the standard is beyond reasonable doubt. In England and Wales, juries are often told they must be sure of guilt. This is a high bar. It does not mean every possible doubt must be ruled out, but any doubt that is reasonable should lead to an acquittal.

Civil law countries often express this as the judge's inner conviction, based on the evidence.

Why so high? Because a criminal conviction can take away someone's freedom. Many legal thinkers argue it is better for some guilty people to go free than for innocent people to be punished.
cards.apply_it: Imagine you are on a jury. What would make you sure, rather than just thinking someone probably did it?

quiz.question: What is the usual standard of proof in criminal cases in common law countries?
options: A majority vote of the public
quiz.explanation: Criminal cases need proof beyond reasonable doubt, a high bar that protects people from wrongful punishment.

cards.title: Criminal cases are about crimes against society, civil cases about private disputes
cards.body:
Courts handle two main types of case.

Criminal cases are brought by the state, usually through a prosecutor, against someone accused of a crime, such as theft, assault or fraud. The case is seen as a wrong against society as a whole. If the accused is found guilty, they can be punished, for example with a fine, community sentence or prison.

Civil cases are disputes between people or organisations. Examples include a broken contract, an unpaid bill, a divorce, a dispute with a landlord or a claim for injury after an accident. The person bringing the case usually wants money, called damages, or an order to make someone do or stop doing something.

The same event can lead to both. A car crash might involve a criminal charge and a civil claim for compensation.
cards.apply_it: Think of a recent dispute in your own life. Would it be a criminal matter, a civil one or neither?

quiz.question: Which is an example of a civil case?
options: A dispute with a landlord over a deposit
quiz.explanation: Civil cases are private disputes, like those over contracts, deposits or injuries, rather than prosecutions for crimes.

cards.title: Civil cases usually use a lower standard: more likely than not
cards.body:
In civil cases, the person bringing the claim usually has to prove their case on the balance of probabilities, or in US terms, by a preponderance of the evidence. Put simply, that means more likely than not.

This is a lower bar than beyond reasonable doubt, because the consequences are usually money or court orders rather than prison.

This explains a famous kind of outcome. In the United States, O. J. Simpson was found not guilty of murder in a criminal trial in 1995. Later, a civil jury found him liable for the deaths and ordered him to pay damages. The two verdicts did not contradict each other. Each court used a different standard of proof.
cards.apply_it: Remember: not guilty in a criminal trial does not always mean a civil case will fail.

quiz.question: Why can someone be found not guilty in a criminal trial but liable in a civil case?
options: Criminal trials are only for fun
The two cases use different standards of proof
quiz.explanation: Criminal cases need proof beyond reasonable doubt, while civil cases need only more likely than not.

cards.title: Prosecutors decide whether there is enough evidence to bring a case
cards.body:
A prosecutor is a lawyer who brings criminal cases on behalf of the state. In England and Wales, this is usually the Crown Prosecution Service. In the US, it is district attorneys and federal prosecutors. Many countries have public prosecutors or state attorneys.

Before going to court, prosecutors usually ask two questions. Is there enough evidence for a realistic chance of conviction? And is prosecution in the public interest? The exact tests differ by country.

Principles like these are meant to stop weak cases wasting time and harming innocent people.

In some civil law countries, investigating judges or magistrates also play a big role in gathering evidence before a trial. In a few systems, victims can bring private prosecutions in limited situations.
cards.apply_it: Find out the name of the main prosecution service in your country.

quiz.question: What two questions do prosecutors in many systems ask before charging?
options: Is there enough evidence, and is prosecution in the public interest?
Is the suspect famous, and is it raining?
Has the suspect paid a fee, and do they have a lawyer?
Is the case on TV, and is the judge free?
quiz.explanation: Prosecutors usually check that evidence is strong enough and that bringing the case serves the public interest.

cards.title: Bail lets many accused people stay free until their trial
cards.body:
After someone is charged, a court decides whether they can stay in the community until their trial or must be held in custody, often called remand.

In many countries, there is a general presumption in favour of bail, because the person has not been convicted. Bail can be refused if there is a serious risk the person will not come back to court, will commit more offences or will interfere with witnesses.

Bail can come with conditions, such as living at a certain address, a curfew, staying away from certain people or reporting to a police station. In some countries, especially the US, courts may require money as a guarantee, which critics say can keep poorer people locked up only because they cannot pay.

Rules on bail are frequently reformed and debated.
cards.apply_it: Think about why holding an innocent person in jail for months before trial could cause real harm.

quiz.question: Why might bail be refused?
options: There is a serious risk they will not attend court or will reoffend
quiz.explanation: Courts may refuse bail if there are real risks such as fleeing, reoffending or interfering with witnesses.

cards.title: Most criminal cases end with a guilty plea, not a full trial
cards.body:
Films focus on dramatic trials, but most criminal cases never reach one. In many countries, the large majority end with the accused pleading guilty.

A guilty plea often leads to a lower sentence than a conviction after trial, because it saves time and spares witnesses. In England and Wales, sentencing guidelines give a reduction of up to one third for an early guilty plea.

In the United States, plea bargaining is very common. The prosecution and defence agree on a charge or sentence in exchange for a guilty plea. The great majority of federal convictions come from guilty pleas.

Supporters say this keeps the system working. Critics worry that the pressure of a much harsher sentence after trial may push some innocent people to plead guilty.
cards.apply_it: Next time you watch a courtroom drama, remember most real cases never get that far.

quiz.question: What is one criticism of plea bargaining?
options: Pressure to accept a deal may lead some innocent people to plead guilty
quiz.explanation: The gap between a plea deal and a possible trial sentence can pressure even innocent people to plead guilty.

cards.title: Some trials are contests between two sides, others are led by the judge
cards.body:
Trials work differently around the world. Two main styles are often described.

In adversarial systems, common in common law countries, the prosecution and defence each present their case, call witnesses and challenge the other side. The judge acts like a referee, making sure the rules are followed. A jury or the judge then decides.

In inquisitorial systems, common in civil law countries like France and Germany, the judge plays a more active role. Judges question witnesses, examine files gathered during the investigation and lead the search for the truth. Lawyers still take part, but with a smaller role.

In reality, many countries mix features of both. Each style has supporters, and researchers debate which is better at finding the truth and protecting rights.
cards.apply_it: If you watch a trial scene in a film, ask yourself: is this adversarial or inquisitorial?

quiz.question: In an inquisitorial system, who usually leads the questioning of witnesses?
quiz.explanation: In inquisitorial systems, judges take an active role, questioning witnesses and leading the inquiry.

cards.title: Judges run the courtroom, explain the law and often decide sentences
cards.body:
Judges have many roles, depending on the country and the court.

In every system, judges make sure proceedings are fair and follow the law. They decide legal questions, such as whether a piece of evidence can be used.

Where there is a jury, the judge explains the law to the jurors and how they should approach the evidence, but the jury decides the facts and the verdict. The judge then usually decides the sentence.

Where there is no jury, the judge, or a panel of judges, decides both the facts and the law. In some countries, professional judges sit alongside trained ordinary citizens called lay judges.

In England and Wales, most minor criminal cases are heard by magistrates, who are often unpaid volunteers from the local community, supported by a legal adviser.
cards.apply_it: Find out whether minor cases in your area are heard by professional judges, volunteers or both.

quiz.question: In a jury trial, who usually decides the sentence?
quiz.explanation: In most jury systems, the jury decides guilt and the judge decides the sentence.

cards.title: Juries let ordinary people decide guilt, but many countries do not use them
cards.body:
A jury is a group of ordinary citizens, chosen at random, who listen to the evidence and decide whether the accused is guilty. In England and Wales and many US states, a criminal jury has 12 members.

Supporters say juries bring community values into the courtroom and protect against unfair laws or prosecutions. Jurors are told to decide only on the evidence presented in court, not on news reports or their own research.

Juries are common in countries influenced by English law, but many countries rarely use them or do not use them at all. Instead, professional judges, sometimes sitting with lay judges, decide cases.

Research on jury decision-making shows that jurors usually take the job seriously, though they can be influenced by bias like anyone else.
cards.apply_it: If you ever get called for jury service, remember to decide only on the evidence heard in court.

quiz.question: What is a jury told to base its decision on?
options: Only the evidence presented in court
quiz.explanation: Jurors must decide only on evidence heard in court, so that the trial is fair to both sides.

cards.title: Defence lawyers make sure the accused gets a fair hearing
cards.body:
The defence lawyer represents the accused. Their job is not to lie or hide the truth, but to test the prosecution's case, protect their client's rights and present the defence.

People sometimes ask how lawyers can defend someone they think is guilty. The answer is that guilt is decided by the court, not the lawyer. A strong defence makes sure the prosecution really proves its case, which protects everyone, including the innocent.

The right to a lawyer is a key part of a fair trial. If someone cannot afford one, many countries provide help called legal aid, or a public defender. How generous this help is varies a great deal, and cuts to legal aid are a common concern.

In common law countries, lawyers may be called solicitors, barristers, attorneys or advocates.
cards.apply_it: Find out how to get free or low-cost legal advice in your area, in case you or a friend ever need it.

quiz.question: Why is it important for guilty-seeming people to have a defence lawyer?
options: So the prosecution must really prove its case, which protects everyone
Because lawyers are paid by the hour
quiz.explanation: A proper defence forces the prosecution to prove its case, which helps prevent innocent people being convicted.

cards.title: Evidence has to meet rules before a court will rely on it
cards.body:
Courts rely on evidence: witness statements, documents, phone records, videos, forensic results and physical objects. But not everything counts.

Many systems have rules about which evidence can be used, called admissibility. Evidence may be excluded if it was gathered illegally, if it is unreliable or if it would be unfairly prejudicial. For example, a confession obtained through threats should not be used.

Common law systems have rules about hearsay, which is when a witness repeats what someone else said outside court. It is often limited, because the original speaker cannot be questioned. But there are many exceptions.

Civil law systems tend to have fewer strict exclusion rules, leaving judges to decide how much weight each piece of evidence deserves.
cards.apply_it: Next time you read about a case, notice what kinds of evidence are mentioned.

quiz.question: What is hearsay?
options: A witness repeating what someone else said outside court
quiz.explanation: Hearsay is second-hand evidence. It is often limited because the person who said it cannot be questioned.

cards.title: Witnesses give evidence under oath and can be questioned by both sides
cards.body:
Witnesses are people who tell the court what they saw, heard or know. They usually promise to tell the truth by taking an oath or making a formal affirmation. Lying in court is a serious crime in most places, often called perjury.

In adversarial systems, a witness is first questioned by the side that called them, then cross-examined by the other side. Cross-examination tests whether the account is accurate, consistent and honest.

Expert witnesses, such as doctors or forensic scientists, explain specialist evidence. Courts must decide how much to trust them.

Many countries now offer special measures for vulnerable witnesses, such as children or victims of sexual offences. These can include giving evidence by video link or behind a screen, so they do not have to face the accused.
cards.apply_it: If you are ever a witness, it is fine to say you do not know or cannot remember. Accuracy matters more than certainty.

quiz.question: What is cross-examination?
options: When a witness is questioned by the other side to test their evidence
When the judge leaves the room
When the accused gives a speech
quiz.explanation: Cross-examination lets the opposing side test a witness's account for accuracy and honesty.

cards.title: Sentencing tries to balance punishment, protection and rehabilitation
cards.body:
When someone is convicted, the court decides the sentence. Sentencing usually tries to achieve several aims at once.

Punishment means giving a penalty that fits the seriousness of the crime. Deterrence aims to discourage the offender and others. Protection keeps the public safe from someone who may be dangerous. Rehabilitation helps the offender change. Reparation means making amends to the victim or community.

These aims can pull in different directions. A long prison sentence may protect the public but make rehabilitation harder. A community sentence may help someone change but feel too light to victims.

Different countries, and different political times, put more weight on different aims. That is one reason sentences for similar crimes can vary so much around the world.
cards.apply_it: Pick a crime you have read about. Which sentencing aim do you think matters most for it, and why?

quiz.question: Which is a common aim of sentencing?
quiz.explanation: Sentencing commonly aims at punishment, deterrence, protection, rehabilitation and reparation.

cards.title: Sentences depend on the crime, the harm and the offender's circumstances
cards.body:
Judges do not usually pick a sentence out of thin air. Many countries set maximum penalties in law, and some have sentencing guidelines. In England and Wales, the Sentencing Council publishes guidelines for judges to follow.

Courts typically look at how much harm was caused and how blameworthy the offender was. Aggravating factors, like using a weapon or targeting a vulnerable person, can increase the sentence. Mitigating factors, like genuine remorse, a first offence or mental health problems, can reduce it.

Possible sentences include discharges, fines, community orders with unpaid work or treatment, suspended sentences and prison. Some countries also use electronic tagging.

A few countries still have the death penalty. Many others have abolished it, and international human rights bodies push for its abolition.
cards.apply_it: Look up whether your country publishes sentencing guidelines online.

quiz.question: What is an aggravating factor?
options: Something that makes a crime more serious, like using a weapon
quiz.explanation: Aggravating factors, such as weapons or targeting vulnerable people, increase the seriousness and the sentence.

cards.title: Restorative justice brings victims and offenders together to repair harm
cards.body:
Restorative justice is an approach that focuses on repairing harm rather than only punishing. With careful preparation and a trained facilitator, it gives victims a chance to meet or communicate with the person who harmed them.

Victims can explain the impact of the crime, ask questions only the offender can answer and sometimes agree on ways to put things right. Offenders have to face the real human cost of what they did.

It is always voluntary, and it is not suitable for every case. It is often used alongside, not instead of, normal sentences.

Research, including reviews of many studies, suggests restorative justice can improve victim satisfaction and may reduce reoffending for some types of crime, though results vary.
cards.apply_it: Think about a time you hurt someone and talking it through helped more than a punishment would have.

quiz.question: What is a key feature of restorative justice?
options: It focuses on repairing harm, often through voluntary contact between victim and offender
It is compulsory for all victims
It is run by the police only
quiz.explanation: Restorative justice is voluntary and focuses on repairing harm, with trained facilitators supporting both sides.

cards.title: Appeals let higher courts correct mistakes
cards.body:
No justice system is perfect, so most allow appeals. An appeal asks a higher court to review a decision made by a lower one.

In criminal cases, a convicted person can usually appeal against their conviction, their sentence or both. In some countries, prosecutors can also appeal, for example against a sentence they think is too lenient.

Appeals are not usually a full rerun of the trial. In many common law systems, appeal courts look mainly at whether there was a legal error, unfairness or new evidence that makes the conviction unsafe. In some civil law systems, appeals can look again at the facts more fully.

There are often time limits for appealing, and permission may be needed. Top courts, like supreme courts, usually only hear cases of wider importance.
cards.apply_it: If you ever face a court decision, remember that appeal deadlines can be short, so legal advice should be sought quickly.

quiz.question: What do appeal courts in many common law systems mainly look for?
options: Whether the jury liked the defendant
Whether the case was on television
Legal errors, unfairness or new evidence that makes a conviction unsafe
quiz.explanation: Appeal courts usually focus on legal mistakes, unfair process or new evidence, rather than rerunning the whole trial.

cards.title: Wrongful convictions happen, often through human error and pressure
cards.body:
Sometimes innocent people are convicted. Organisations that study exonerations, such as the US National Registry of Exonerations, have recorded thousands of cases where convictions were later overturned.

Common causes include mistaken eyewitness identification, false confessions after long or pressured interviews, unreliable or misleading forensic evidence, dishonest informants, and misconduct by officials, such as hiding evidence that would help the defence.

Weak legal representation and pressure to accept plea deals can also play a part.

Wrongful convictions are a double harm. An innocent person is punished, and the real offender may remain free to hurt others. They also damage public trust in justice. Reborn's guide How Crimes Get Solved explains more about how investigations can go wrong.
cards.apply_it: Remember that a conviction is a human decision, and even careful systems can make mistakes.

quiz.question: Which is a common cause of wrongful convictions?
quiz.explanation: Mistaken eyewitnesses, false confessions and unreliable forensics are among the most common causes.

cards.title: Review bodies and innocence projects help correct wrongful convictions
cards.body:
Because appeals can fail even when a conviction is wrong, some countries have created extra safeguards.

In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, the Criminal Cases Review Commission is an independent body that can investigate possible miscarriages of justice and send cases back to the Court of Appeal. Scotland, Norway and New Zealand have similar bodies.

In the US and elsewhere, innocence projects, often linked to law schools, investigate claims of innocence. DNA testing has helped free many wrongly convicted people.

Cases like these have led to reforms. Examples include recording police interviews, improving eyewitness line-up procedures, requiring prosecutors to share evidence with the defence and raising standards for forensic science.

These changes do not end every mistake, but they reduce the risk.
cards.apply_it: Look up whether your country has an independent body that reviews possible miscarriages of justice.

quiz.question: What does the Criminal Cases Review Commission do?
options: Investigates possible miscarriages of justice and can refer cases to an appeal court
quiz.explanation: The CCRC independently reviews possible wrongful convictions and can send cases back to the Court of Appeal.

cards.title: Young people are usually treated differently, but the age varies widely
cards.body:
Most countries have special rules for children and teenagers who break the law. They usually go to youth courts, have their identities protected and receive sentences more focused on education and rehabilitation.

The age of criminal responsibility, below which children cannot be prosecuted, varies widely. In England and Wales, it is 10. In Scotland, it is 12. In many European countries, such as Germany, it is 14, and in some Nordic countries it is 15. In the US, it depends on the state.

The United Nations Committee on the Rights of the Child encourages countries to set it at 14 or higher.

These differences reflect different views about how much young children understand their actions and how best to respond to harmful behaviour.
cards.apply_it: Find out the age of criminal responsibility where you live, and whether you think it is right.

quiz.question: What does the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child encourage as a minimum age of criminal responsibility?
quiz.explanation: The committee encourages countries to set the minimum age of criminal responsibility at 14 or higher.

cards.title: Justice looks different around the world, and international courts exist too
cards.body:
Beyond the differences already covered, countries vary in many ways. Some allow cameras in court, others ban them. Some have elected judges, others appoint them. Prison rates vary hugely, with some countries imprisoning many times more people per head than others.

The death penalty is one of the sharpest differences. Amnesty International reports that most countries have abolished it in law or practice, while a minority still carry out executions.

There are also international courts. The International Criminal Court in The Hague can try people accused of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity, when national courts are unable or unwilling to. Not every country accepts its authority. The International Court of Justice settles disputes between states.

Regional courts, like the European Court of Human Rights, hear complaints that states have breached human rights.
cards.apply_it: Read about one country's justice system that is very different from yours.

quiz.question: What kinds of crime can the International Criminal Court try?
options: Genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity
quiz.explanation: The ICC focuses on the gravest crimes, such as genocide and war crimes, when national courts cannot or will not act.

cards.title: Knowing the basics helps you understand the news and protect your rights
cards.body:
Justice systems differ widely, but many share the same core ideas. The law should apply to everyone. Judges should be independent. People are presumed innocent, and the prosecution must prove guilt, usually beyond reasonable doubt. Criminal and civil cases use different standards. Evidence and witnesses are tested before anyone is convicted. Sentences try to balance punishment, protection and rehabilitation. Appeals and review bodies exist because mistakes happen.

Understanding these ideas helps you read the news more critically, serve well on a jury and know when to seek help.

Remember, this guide is general education, not legal advice. If you ever face a legal problem, contact a qualified lawyer, a legal aid service or a free advice centre in your country as soon as you can.
cards.apply_it: Save the details of one free legal advice service in your area, just in case.

quiz.question: If you face a real legal problem, what should you do?
options: Rely only on a general guide
Seek advice from a qualified lawyer or legal advice service
Ask a stranger online to decide
quiz.explanation: General knowledge helps, but rules vary by place, so real legal problems need advice from a qualified professional.
